candidateRows: Contingent reality is best explained by a noncontingent, automatically actual foundation rather than by another contingent member or no explanation.
This is the initial formulation of the contingency argument and directly supplies its explanatory premise, anti-circularity step, and necessary-foundation conclusion.
After introductory framing, Rasmussen presents the debate's principal affirmative case by defining contingent things and tracing their ultimate explanation beyond the contingent collection.
The argument can initially leave necessity somewhat open while still inferring a noncontingent source from the need to explain contingent reality without circularity.
The move defends the inference against conceptual ambiguity by separating the core explanatory structure from a fully specified account of necessity.
Clifton's concern that the conclusion invokes an unclear notion of a necessary being.
Rasmussen answers the request for modal clarification by treating automatically actual existence as a provisional concept and restating the anti-circular explanatory inference.
Explanatory intuitions that apply to ordinary contingent objects need not extend to material reality as a whole, whose existence may instead be brute.
This directly challenges the argument's extrapolation from local explanations to ultimate reality and rejects the need for a necessarily existing foundation.
Rasmussen's inference from explanations of ordinary contingent things to a noncontingent source of all contingent reality.
Clifton grants that ordinary collections invite noncircular explanations but argues that his explanatory intuition fails at the level of all material reality and possible worlds.
Necessity admits stronger and weaker senses, allowing the foundational conclusion to avoid implausible logical certainty while retaining a substantive form of automatic actuality.
The distinctions answer a central modal objection and preserve a version of the necessary-foundation conclusion that does not require the strongest conceivable necessity.
Clifton's claim that conceivable Godless worlds make a necessarily existing being difficult to accept.
Rasmussen distinguishes logical or epistemic certainty from factual and weaker necessities, seeking common ground before asking how strongly a foundational reality must exist.
Even if the universe has a first temporal moment and is contingent, its brute existence remains plausible because causal intuitions may not govern the temporal boundary.
The move grants much of the pro side's setup while denying its decisive explanatory premise, offering brute contingency as the main rival account.
The stage-one claim that contingent reality requires some necessary or automatically actual foundational layer.
Clifton separates having a cosmic beginning from coming into existence within time and argues that ordinary causal expectations may fail at the universe's boundary.
The same disciplined explanatory reasoning used in ordinary inquiry and science supports preferring an available noncontingent explanation of contingent reality over brute existence.
This supplies the affirmative answer to the brute-fact alternative by grounding the contingency inference in general explanatory practice and comparative probability.
Clifton's proposal that the universe may be a brute fact beyond the reach of ordinary causal and explanatory intuitions.
Rasmussen affirms epistemic humility but argues that some truths about ultimate reality remain accessible and that available explanations can rationally outrank no explanation.
Calling a foundation necessarily existent does not itself explain why it exists, because the property of necessity applies only given the thing's existence.
The objection attacks the proposed foundation's explanatory advantage by arguing that necessity merely redescribes its existence instead of accounting for it.
Rasmussen's contention that an automatically actual foundation supplies a better ultimate explanation than brute contingent reality.
Clifton accepts the desire for explanation but questions how divine necessity improves understanding when the alleged necessary property presupposes the foundation already exists.
Necessity fails as an explanation of divine existence in the same way that a result cannot explain its own antecedent cause merely by being required for that result.
The analogy sharpens the prior objection by alleging explanatory reversal and identifies why necessity seems conditional on, rather than explanatory of, existence.
The proposal that a necessary status can explain why the foundational or divine reality exists.
Following the moderator's clarification, Clifton says necessity is unsatisfying and uses a causal analogy to argue that the proposed explanatory direction runs backward.
Things that could have failed to be actual especially call for explanation, whereas a necessarily or automatically actual foundation does not raise that same explanatory demand.
This is the affirmative side's principal response to the claim that necessary existence is explanatorily idle, distinguishing contingent from automatic actuality.
Clifton's objection that necessity cannot explain existence and instead reverses the proper direction of explanation.
Rasmussen argues that explanatory demand tracks possible nonactuality, then suggests that a supreme nature may further illuminate necessity while leaving contingent causation for later analysis.
Explaining necessity by divine supremacy appears circular if necessary existence is itself one of the properties that constitutes or produces that supremacy.
The move challenges the proposed deeper explanation of the foundation's necessity by arguing that supremacy and necessity cannot explain each other without circularity.
Rasmussen's suggestion that the foundation's supreme nature may explain or predict its necessarily actual character.
Clifton contends that necessity is normally treated as greatness-making, so invoking supremacy to explain necessity reverses their dependence and invites a further explanatory question.
Explaining divine necessity by divine supremacy appears circular because necessary existence is itself a property contributing to supremacy.
The objection directly challenges the proposed explanation of the foundation's necessity and presses whether the account reverses its explanatory direction.
Rasmussen's suggestion that the supreme nature of the foundation explains or predicts its necessary existence.
Rasmussen had suggested that supremacy might explain necessity; Clifton argues that necessity already helps constitute supremacy and asks what fact makes the necessity obtain.
A necessary foundation may require no deeper explanation precisely because its existence is automatically actual and cannot fail to obtain.
This supplies the central stopping-point defense of the contingency argument by explaining why inquiry may legitimately terminate at necessary reality.
Clifton's challenge asking what fact makes the foundation's existence necessary and whether supremacy can provide that explanation.
In response to the circularity concern, Rasmussen allows either a supremacy-based explanation or no further explanation once reality bottoms out in something automatically actual.
For any contingent things there is an explanation of their existence, and that explanation cannot itself belong among the contingent things explained.
This states the operative contingency principle and the inference by which an explanation of contingent reality must lie beyond the contingent collection.
After discussion of alternative causal principles, Rasmussen gives a streamlined formulation covering any contingent plurality and draws the foundational inference from it.
Brute contingency is explanatorily worse than brute necessity because a contingent ultimate still seems open to a deeper noncontingent explanation.
The comparison provides the principal abductive reason for preferring a necessary foundation over an unexplained contingent terminus of reality.
Clifton's concern that a necessary foundation may be no less brute or explanation-demanding than a contingent foundation.
Using an automatically actual foundational reality rather than a specifically divine example, Rasmussen argues that necessity removes the distinctive demand for a deeper explanation.
Contingency as nonexistence in some possible worlds need not imply dependence, since an independent God could still fail to exist in some worlds.
The distinction attacks a key bridge from modal contingency to explanatory dependence and permits an independent yet nonnecessary ultimate reality.
Rasmussen's treatment of a merely contingent ultimate as thereby calling for explanation in terms of something noncontingent.
Clifton warns that different senses of contingency are being conflated and proposes that world-relative divine existence could be brute without making God dependent.
An objective and necessary logical landscape can belong to reality's foundation, with human reasoning tracking rules that remain true independently of minds.
The proposal supplies a substantive model of automatically actual reality and links necessary logical structure to the foundation reached by contingency reasoning.
Rasmussen develops a mind-independent realm of logical rules, argues that it has ontological necessity, and suggests those rules are woven into a supreme foundation.
Logical laws may regulate statements and inference rather than constitute a mind-independent ontological structure embedded in reality itself.
The objection contests the principal example offered to make necessary foundational reality intelligible and weakens the proposed route from logic to ontology.
Rasmussen's claim that necessary rules of logic form an objective logical landscape within the fabric of reality's foundation.
Clifton accepts that the universe is what it is but doubts that laws of logic exist outside language as entities or constraints binding the world.
Propositional content survives the removal of particular minds and inscriptions, supporting necessary abstract reality that a concrete foundation could unify within its nature.
The argument defends mind-independent necessary content and then integrates abstract necessity with the proposed concrete necessary foundation of contingent reality.
Clifton's claim that logic applies only through statements and his thought experiment separating valid inference from the world's own structure.
Rasmussen argues that identical propositional content transcends minds, chalkboards, and symbols, then presents its integration with a concrete necessary being as explanatorily unified.
Necessary mathematical propositions have intelligible truth-makers, whereas no analogous fact appears to make a concrete God incapable of nonexistence.
This directly challenges the inference from acknowledged abstract necessities to a necessarily existing concrete foundation by identifying an explanatory asymmetry.
Rasmussen's attempt to connect necessarily existing abstract propositions with a unified concrete necessary foundation.
Clifton says mathematical necessity can be explained through the incoherence of denial, but he sees nothing doing equivalent work for the claim that God cannot fail to exist.

Contradictions can emerge only through extended inference, so conceivability of a godless world does not establish its possibility, while contingency reasoning may independently indicate hidden impossibility.
The response undercuts the modal premise behind Clifton's contingent-God proposal and assigns the contingency argument an independent role in revealing necessity.
Clifton's argument that concrete divine necessity lacks the contradiction-based explanation available for necessary mathematical propositions.
Rasmussen uses propositions about nothingness and thought to show that contradictions may require several inferential steps, then denies that easy conceivability settles genuine possibility.
An undecided mathematical conjecture can have a contradictory truth or falsity even when nobody is yet able to recognize the contradiction.
The example directly supports the possibility of logically contradictory propositions whose contradictory character remains outside current human recognition.
Scott Clifton's attempt to deny that an unrecognized false identity statement is genuinely contradictory.
After accepting that the consciousness identity example may favor Clifton, Rasmussen substitutes an unproved mathematical conjecture to defend unseen contradiction.
A foundational reality may simply be brute, and moving from its lack of further explanation to existence in every possible world is unwarranted.
This challenges the contingency argument's crucial transition from an unexplained foundation to a metaphysically necessary foundation or necessary God.
Rasmussen's case that the explanatory foundation has necessity comparable to the necessity associated with logic.
Clifton grants substantial agreement about a foundation but argues that brute existence need not entail existence across all possible worlds.
Calling the foundation brute means only that it has no further explanation, while a necessary nature can still distinguish it from dependent contingent objects.
The clarification blocks an equivocation between brute and contingent and preserves necessity as the proposed differentiator of the foundational reality.
Clifton's treatment of a brute foundation as something that merely happens to exist rather than existing necessarily.
Rasmussen responds that absence of further explanation does not itself imply contingency and says necessary nature separates a foundation from ordinary dependent things.
Necessary existence does not explain why God exists, and any acceptable brute-foundation status available to God appears equally available to the universe.
The move attacks necessity's explanatory value and argues that the pro side has not established a principled advantage for God over a brute universe.
Rasmussen's clarification that necessary nature explains how the foundation differs from dependent contingent objects.
Clifton argues that necessity supplies no understanding of divine existence and contrasts a brute status shared with the universe against a stronger necessity he rejects.
A merely contingent foundation would remain apt for further explanation, so explanatory improvement gives reason to attribute a more robust nature to reality's foundation.
This supplies the positive explanatory inference from contingent reality toward a robust foundational nature while postponing further claims about deity or supremacy.
Clifton's contention that brute foundational status fits the universe and that stronger necessity lacks adequate support.
Rasmussen reframes the inquiry around the universe's foundation and argues that a conceivable better explanation counts against its being merely contingent.
The proposed foundation should remain in the contingent category because concrete beings do not appear capable of necessity, unlike possibly abstract propositions.
The objection identifies the skeptic's underlying modal boundary: necessity may apply to abstracta but not to a concrete foundational being.
Rasmussen's inference that the explanatory foundation has a more robust nature than ordinary contingent objects.
Clifton says he would place the foundation back among contingent things because he cannot see how a concrete being could possess necessary existence.
Resistance to a necessary concrete foundation may arise from picturing concrete reality as material, whereas God may be an immaterial conceptual mind with causal powers.
The move answers the modal intuition against concrete necessity by separating concreteness from material composition and proposing an alternative kind of causal reality.
Clifton's claim that the foundation must be contingent because no concrete being appears capable of necessary existence.
Rasmussen suggests that material imagery drives Clifton's resistance and describes the proposed foundation as conceptual, personal, immaterial, and causally efficacious.
Even after granting the existence of immaterial concrete entities, the skeptical objection that such entities remain contingent still stands.
The concession neutralizes Rasmussen's proposed diagnosis and shows that distinguishing immaterial from material reality does not resolve the modal dispute.
Rasmussen's diagnosis that Clifton's rejection of necessary concrete reality may depend on imagining all concrete things as material.
Clifton accepts nonmaterial concrete entities and insists that his resistance to their necessary existence survives that conceptual distinction.
The contingency argument can be persuasive without rationally compelling everyone, as people may accept its premises and be moved toward a necessary being.
This explicitly answers the debate motion by distinguishing an argument's capacity to rationally move some people from its capacity to force universal assent.
In closing, Rasmussen says the argument moved him and some surveyed nonbelievers while emphasizing that an unpersuaded person may remain fully rational.
Treating propositions as mind-independent existing things remains implausible, though granting that ontology would provide a basis for further discussion about a personal foundation.
The move locates his remaining resistance in the ontology of abstract propositions while identifying the conditional progress available if that premise were granted.
Rasmussen's use of abstract logical or propositional reality to support a necessary conceptual foundation and a second-stage inquiry.
Clifton remains unconvinced that propositions exist independently, but concedes that accepting them would make further inquiry into the foundation less problematic.
